name: Price, income and cross elasticities of demand

terms.definition: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in a good's own price, measured as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
terms.examiner: The two-step method is what scores: calculate both percentage changes first, then divide. Reports say the students who lost marks skipped straight to the division or forgot the minus sign.

terms.definition: A PED between 0 and −1: quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price, so a price rise increases total revenue.
terms.examiner: The petrol question (PED −0.2) was answered best by students who drew a steep demand curve and then talked about revenue; naming 'inelastic' alone earned one mark.

terms.definition: A PED more negative than −1: quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price, so a price cut increases total revenue.
terms.examiner: Say what it means for revenue, not just for quantity. 'Elastic so demand falls a lot' is description; the mark is for the revenue consequence.

terms.definition: A PED of exactly −1: a change in price leaves total revenue unchanged because quantity changes by the same percentage.
terms.examiner: Rare as a direct question but a common end-point of 'explain how a firm could maximise revenue'.

terms.definition: Price multiplied by quantity sold. The direction it moves after a price change depends on PED.
terms.examiner: A mark was lost by a run of students for writing the revenue figure without its units ('million'). Write the full number with its unit.

terms.definition: Availability of close substitutes, proportion of income spent on the good, whether it is a necessity or a luxury, whether it is addictive or habit-forming, and the time period considered.
terms.examiner: The bus-ticket question asked for one reason for a difference in PED between two groups: the top answers picked one determinant and linked it to those particular consumers.

terms.definition: The responsiveness of demand to a change in consumers' real income, measured as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income.
terms.examiner: The sign tells you the type of good; the size tells you how much demand will swing in a recession or a boom. Both are needed for the 'significance to the producer' questions.

terms.definition: A good with positive YED: demand rises as income rises. A luxury is a normal good with YED greater than +1; a necessity has YED between 0 and +1.
terms.examiner: Students could define normal and inferior goods but then failed to use the data to decide which the good was. Quote the figures and show the direction.

terms.definition: A good with negative YED: demand falls as income rises, because consumers switch to better alternatives.
terms.examiner: In the Freddo question many identified the chocolate bar as normal when the stem pointed to inferior. Read the extract for the clue before deciding.

terms.definition: The responsiveness of demand for one good to a change in the price of another, measured as the percentage change in quantity demanded of good A divided by the percentage change in the price of good B.
terms.examiner: Half the marks in the gaming-machine question were for saying what a value of +1.28 means: the goods are substitutes and the response is more than proportionate.

terms.definition: Goods that can replace each other in consumption, so they have a positive XED: a rise in the price of one raises demand for the other.
terms.examiner: Give an example from the data when the question offers one; the four-mark substitutes-and-complements question rewarded examples as well as definitions.

terms.definition: Goods consumed together, so they have a negative XED: a rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other.
terms.examiner: The fish-and-chips calculation (XED −8) was mostly done correctly; errors came from applying the percentage to the wrong good's quantity.

terms.definition: The change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100. Every elasticity calculation begins with two of these.
terms.examiner: Dividing by the new value rather than the original is the commonest slip in the bank's elasticity calculations.

terms.definition: The more price inelastic demand is, the larger the share of an indirect tax that falls on consumers rather than producers.
terms.examiner: This is the link that turns a Theme 1 definition into Level 3 analysis on tax questions: state it and then show it on the diagram.

terms.definition: Demand tends to become more price elastic in the long run because consumers have time to find substitutes and change habits.
terms.examiner: A ready-made evaluation point for any question about the effect of a price change or a tax.
